subject: knight
pitch: A fantasy knight in battle-worn plate armour. A great helm with a narrow eye slit and a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates etched with gold filigree, a deep-blue surcoat with a silver griffin emblem, a tall kite shield bearing the same griffin, and a broadsword. Dents and scratches tell of many battles, and a torn crimson cape hangs from the shoulders.
reasoning:
I'm planning a fantasy knight model using the agentic-3js-builder SDK, thinking through realistic human proportions for a knight in full plate with a great helm and plume, aiming for roughly 1.9-2.1 meters tall.

For the rig, I need a humanoid skeleton with hips as root, branching into spine/neck/head and limb chains for legs and arms. Rather than a strict T-pose, I'm considering a slightly asymmetric stance — shield arm raised holding the shield forward, sword arm relaxed at the side with the blade — to make the rest pose feel more character-appropriate while still staying readable for rigging purposes.

Now I'm reviewing the builder API carefully since I can't execute code to verify it: joints need parent/aim/direction parameters, chains use path functions like polyline or catmull, and parts attach geometry to bones with position, orientation and scale options, plus helpers like sweep, rod, and capsule for generating tube-like or capsule shapes. I want to make sure I use these signatures correctly so the module doesn't break.

I'm also noting other helpers like `svg`, `rng`, `frame`, `line`, `mix`, `DEG`, `aim`, `limb`, and `Surface` from their respective modules. For the gold filigree on shoulder plates, I'm thinking through how to apply an svg texture decal with a tinted gold color while still preserving the base plate color, considering whether a textured material with vertex colors would work better than a plain tint.

Since alphaTest cuts away transparent texture regions, I realize a simple textured mesh would hide the base plate beneath it, so I'm leaning toward using the `decal()` function to apply the filigree as a thin overlay sheet on the curved pauldron surface instead. I'm also thinking about how to render the griffin emblem on the surcoat and shield — likely a hand-drawn SVG silhouette path approximating a heraldic rampant griffin, tinted silver.

I'll build the griffin SVG from simple shapes — an ellipse body, circular head with a beak triangle, wing paths, leg paths, and a tail — sized for a viewBox and scaled down so it still reads clearly on a shield roughly 0.3m across. For the surcoat, I'm weighing whether to apply the emblem via a decal on the torso's chest surface or treat the surcoat as a separate layered mesh.

Thinking through the decal mechanics: I need the torso meshes built first, then place the decal with a centre point and outward-facing direction, sizing it to fit the chest, and making sure the ray origin sits behind the surface so it projects correctly onto the front.

For the surcoat itself, I'm treating it as a tabard worn over the cuirass—covering the chest and hanging to the thighs, with the emblem decal placed on its front, slightly larger than the plate armor underneath.

Now I'm sketching overall proportions: total height around 2.0 m including helm and plume, feet planted at y=0, keeping the stylized blocky look while deciding how exaggerated the head size should be.

I'm mapping out the body's vertical joint heights from feet to plume tip, plus the great helm's dimensions as a flat-topped cylinder sitting atop the shoulders since it fully encloses the head. Then I'm planning the skeleton rig—hips as root, a spine chain up to the neck and head, plus leg and arm chains—to properly build this humanoid knight joint by joint.

Setting up leg joints and capsule geometry...

Now I'm planning the limb parts to use cylinder geometry oriented via the `aim` parameter toward each joint, with explicit `bone` assignments so thighs and shins attach to the correct hip/knee segments. I'm sketching the overall skeleton hierarchy, starting with the hips joint and building a spine chain upward through several named vertebra joints.

Still defining joints...

Tracing through how createChain resolves parents is tricky — boneFor always requires an existing joint via nearestJoint, so a chain can't be the very first thing created without throwing. That means I need a root "hips" joint created first, but then the spine chain's first span joint at t=0 would just duplicate that same position, which feels redundant.

Let me think about spans and names more carefully: for a polyline with N points there are N-1 spans, and the names array length determines whether we get span joints only or span joints plus a tip joint. If I define the spine as a single-span polyline from waist to chest with two names, the span joint lands at t=0 (the waist position) and the tip lands at chest — so the waist joint sits right at the pelvis height, which is close to but not exactly the hips position.

Rather than overthinking this, I'll just build the humanoid rig manually with individual joints: hips, waist, chest, neck, head, each specified with explicit positions and a parent, and reserve chains for the tails, tentacles, and legs where repetition makes sense.

For each leg I'll construct a chain from a polyline through hip, knee, ankle, and toe points, naming each span joint (hipL, kneeL, ankleL) with toeL as the tip, then sweep a mesh for the thigh segment using the chain's own joints.

For rigid armor plates though, I'm considering whether to use explicit bones with capsule sweeps between joint endpoints instead of a continuously smooth sweep, since passing a joint as a point input gives it proper weights for binding.

Thinking through cuisses and greaves, I'm planning to use tapered cylinder parts with explicit bone assignment, positioned at the midpoint between joints and aimed toward the next joint so the geometry's axis points along the limb direction.

Now I'm working out the full knight design piece by piece, starting with the great helm as a cylinder with a flat top, plus a dark recessed box for the eye slit and small dark breathing holes on the front.

I'm also adding a thin torus for a gold trim rim around the helm's base, then thinking through how to construct the tall crimson plume — considering a curved sweep or extruded fin shape so it reads well as a feather-like crest rising from the top of the helm.

I'm reconsidering the plume as an extruded silhouette oriented so its broad crest reads properly from the front view, since a simple sweep would look too thin from that angle — the outline needs to show vertical height and width along the default viewing axis rather than just depth.

As a fuller alternative, I'm weighing a card-based approach: building the plume from a series of textured feather cards arranged along a curve from the helm top, each with an SVG-drawn tapered feather shape in crimson, which could give a more convincing feathered look than a solid extrusion.

Now I'm working out the orientation logic for cards on frames — how the card's spine and width axes relate to the frame's facing and flow directions so each feather card tilts and fans correctly along the plume's curve.

Working through the math, lean=90 with flow along Y and facing Z gives a vertical card in the XY plane facing the viewer — that's the configuration I want. Given the complexity, I'm leaning toward a simpler approach: a sweep-based plume core, or maybe a flat extruded fan shape (narrow base, ragged widening top) positioned on the helm crest, which should read as a tall crimson plume without all the frame math.

I'm liking the ragged, torn-edge look for a battle-worn feel, and I'll add a second thin extrusion layer offset slightly for depth, plus a gold torus collar at the base where it attaches to the helm. One main plate facing front with a ragged top edge should read convincingly as a plume even though it's flat in profile, and I can layer a second offset outline on the same plane for extra volume rather than overcomplicating with multiple rotated plates.

Working out the correct orientation vectors so the plate faces outward properly, then sketching the ragged fan-shaped outline point by point, rising from a narrow base to a notched, jagged top edge.

I'm placing the plume's bottom at the helm's top so the total figure height stays near real-world proportions (~2 m), then sketching the helm as a cylinder sitting on a gorget ring at the neck -- helm centered around y=1.65 with the gorget just below it.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy: hips as root, a spine chain running from hips up through waist to chest, and a head joint for the helm. Deciding to orient the blade so width runs along X and length along the sword axis, with thickness along Z, so the flat face reads clearly from the front. Now sketching the tapering outline points for the broadsword blade shape, narrow at the base and coming to a point at the tip.

Attaching the sword to the "handR" bone on the figure's right hand, since that's a chain-tip joint well-suited for rigid attachment, and setting the extrude's "at" to the guard position so the blade extends from the guard outward to the tip along the computed axis direction.

I'm computing the guard and tip positions in world space relative to the hand joint, normalizing the blade axis vector, and working out the crossguard orientation so it sits perpendicular to the blade in the flat plane.

Working out the crossguard dimensions so it lies flat in the blade plane, then figuring out the grip cylinder and pommel sphere positions relative to the guard point, stepping along the blade direction to place each part correctly.

For the grip, I'm considering using a rod/sweep between two endpoints with an explicit bone binding, since the default weight resolution would just pick the nearest joint—better to specify `{bone: "handR"}` directly. I'm also thinking rods or capsules could work well for limb segments, and wondering whether to model arms as bendable chains with sweep meshes versus rigid armored pieces.

Now I'm settling on using named chains for the arm and leg rigs, giving the limb segments roles so the joints double as both rig structure and mesh-generation points, which keeps the code simpler than defining separate joints and parts.

I'm now working out actual coordinates—placing the pelvis root, then defining the leg chains symmetrically with hip, knee, ankle, and toe joint positions on each side, parented to the hips.

Next I'm figuring out the foot and leg armor pieces: a box for the sabaton foot sitting at the ankle so its bottom touches the ground plane, and a tapered cylinder greave running from knee to ankle.

For the thigh cuisse, I'm working out a cylinder from hip to knee, aimed along its direction and tapered slightly between top and bottom radii, confirming each leg span is "owned" by its upper joint for bone attachment purposes.

For the knee I'm placing a small sphere as a plate covering the joint, keeping it simple with b.part rather than a sweep. I'm planning to use parts (cylinders, boxes, spheres) for most limbs since they're predictable, reserving membrane sweeps for things like the torn cape and plume — defining the cape as a membrane stretched between a curved top edge over the shoulders and a ragged bottom edge lower on the back, positioned slightly behind the torso.

For the jagged cape bottom, I'm figuring out how to sample a zigzag polyline by arc length against a smooth top edge, using enough columns in the membrane grid to capture the teeth of the tear without losing the notch shape.

I'm also deciding to rig the whole cape rigidly to the chest joint so it doesn't bend with body motion, and planning a crimson mottled weave texture for the fabric paint at a thin 0.01 thickness, while confirming the membrane edges can just take plain point arrays instead of full Path objects.

For construction, I'm now sketching the surcoat as a front tabard panel built with extrude: a trapezoid outline from the shoulders down to a flared, split hem, set as a thin plate positioned just in front of the breastplate.

I'm reconsidering whether the surcoat needs both front and back panels or just a front one, since the cape covers the rear — maybe instead a full lofted body shape wrapping the torso would read more naturally, with the loft rigged to the spine chain so it follows the body's bone structure while flaring slightly toward the hem.
